steps.tx: Mitz and Peyronie defined the **superficial musculoaponeurotic system** or SMAS in 1976 as a continuous fibroaponeurotic network investing the mimetic muscles of the face. The SMAS is continuous superiorly with the temporoparietal fascia (galea) and inferiorly with the platysma muscle in the neck.
steps.say: Surgeons identify that mitz and Peyronie identified the superficial musculoaponeurotic system as a fibroaponeurotic layer continuous with the galea superiorly and platysma inferiorly.

nodes.label: Superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) in the cheek
Platysma muscle extending into the neck

steps.tx: True osteocutaneous **facial retaining ligaments** anchor the overlying soft tissues and skin firmly to the facial skeleton. The zygomatic retaining ligament (McGregor patch) and mandibular retaining ligament must be surgically released during deep-plane or extended SMAS dissection to mobilize midfacial soft tissues.
steps.say: Surgeons identify that true facial retaining ligaments anchor the soft tissues to the underlying facial skeleton. Surgeons identify that the zygomatic and mandibular retaining ligaments must be released to mobilize midfacial tissues.

rows: Arise directly from bone into the dermis
Arise from deep fascia into the dermis

steps.tx: Facelift surgical planes encompass subcutaneous skin-only undermining, SMAS plication or imbrication, and the **deep plane rhytidectomy**. Popularized by Hamra, deep plane rhytidectomy enters the avascular sub-SMAS plane, releasing the retaining ligaments and repositioning the composite malar fat pad, midface, and platysma.
steps.say: Surgeons identify that surgeons identify that facelift techniques range from skin-only lifts to deep plane rhytidectomy. Surgeons identify that deep plane dissection elevates the SMAS, malar fat, and platysma as a composite unit without skin tension.

left.title: Subcutaneous Skin Lift
points: High skin tension and wide scars
Prone to windswept deformity and early relapse

right.title: Deep Plane Rhytidectomy
points: Tension borne entirely by deep fascia

steps.tx: Anterior neck laxity and prominent platysma bands are addressed via a submental incision. An **anterior platysmaplasty** reapproximates the separated medial platysma borders using a midline corset suturing technique, combined with subplatysmal fat excision and partial transverse transection of platysma bands to deepen the cervicomental angle.
steps.say: Platysma bands are corrected through a submental incision. Surgeons identify that anterior platysmaplasty reapproximates medial muscle borders with a corset technique to deepen the cervicomental angle.

nodes.label: Submental incision and submental skin flap elevation
Midline corset platysmaplasty and lateral SMAS suspension

steps.tx: The **great auricular nerve** is the most commonly injured nerve during rhytidectomy, vulnerable as it crosses superficial to the sternocleidomastoid muscle. McKinney landmark locates the nerve 6.5 cm below the external auditory meatus at the midpoint of the muscle belly, requiring careful superficial dissection.
steps.say: The great auricular nerve is the most frequently injured nerve in rhytidectomy. Surgeons identify that surgeons identify that it crosses the sternocleidomastoid muscle six and a half centimeters below the external acoustic meatus.

vis.alt: Metzenbaum scissors for delicate postauricular nerve dissection
vis.caption: Surgical instruments for protecting the great auricular nerve over sternocleidomastoid. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.tx: Motor nerve branches of the facial nerve are safeguarded by adhering strictly to anatomical planes. The **frontal branch of the facial nerve** runs in the sub-temporoparietal fascia plane, crossing the zygomatic arch 1.5 cm anterior to the tragus along the Pitanguy line, demanding dissection deep to the deep temporal fascia.
steps.say: Surgeons identify that surgeons identify that the frontal branch of the facial nerve runs along the Pitanguy line over the zygomatic arch. Surgeons identify that surgeons identify that dissection above the arch must remain deep to the deep temporal fascia to prevent brow ptosis.

rows: Crosses facial vessels at mandible border
Deep to platysma and superficial layer of cervical fascia
Travel superficial to buccal fat pad

steps.tx: An expanding **major hematoma** represents the single most common early acute surgical complication of rhytidectomy, developing in 1% to 3% of operative cases and presenting with sudden severe pain, unilateral swelling, and dermal ecchymosis. Immediate bedside stitch removal and surgical evacuation are mandatory to prevent skin flap ischaemic necrosis.
steps.say: Expanding hematoma is the most common acute complication after facelift. Surgeons identify that sudden unilateral pain and swelling require urgent suture release and hematoma evacuation to prevent flap necrosis.

right.title: Small Stable Seroma
points: Managed with needle aspiration and compression

steps.tx: Perioperative blood pressure control is the single most critical factor in reducing post-rhytidectomy hematoma risk. Maintaining systolic blood pressure strictly under **140 mmHg** before induction, intraoperatively, and throughout the initial 48 hours postoperatively decreases haematoma occurrence by more than half.
steps.say: Controlling blood pressure is the key factor preventing hematoma. Maintaining systolic pressure strictly below one hundred forty millimeters of mercury reduces hematoma risk by over half.
